lessons.title: Homeostasis and the Nervous System
lessons.description: How the body maintains stable internal conditions, and the structure of the nervous system.
lessons.content_html:
Homeostasis

Homeostasis is the regulation of the internal conditions of the body to maintain a stable environment. This is essential because cells need the right conditions to function properly — particularly for enzyme action. The conditions controlled include body temperature, blood glucose concentration, water levels and ion levels.

Key Fact

Homeostasis maintains optimal internal conditions for enzyme activity. All control systems involve: receptors (detect stimuli), coordination centres (brain, spinal cord, pancreas) and effectors (muscles or glands that produce a response).

Homeostatic control systems involve three components: receptors that detect changes in the environment (stimuli), coordination centres (the brain, spinal cord and pancreas) that receive and process information, and effectors (muscles and glands) that carry out a response. Many homeostatic systems use negative feedback — a mechanism where the response works to reverse the change and return conditions to the optimum.

The Nervous System

The nervous system enables humans to react to their surroundings and coordinate behaviour. It is made up of the central nervous system (CNS) — the brain and spinal cord — and the peripheral nervous system (sensory and motor neurones that connect receptors and effectors to the CNS).

The pathway of a nervous response is: stimulus → receptor → sensory neurone → relay neurone (in CNS) → motor neurone → effector → response.

Neurones do not directly touch each other. The tiny gap between two neurones is called a synapse. When an electrical impulse reaches the end of a neurone, it triggers the release of chemical neurotransmitters that diffuse across the gap and bind to receptors on the next neurone, triggering a new electrical impulse. This allows signals to pass between neurones.

Reflex Actions

Reflex actions are rapid, automatic responses that do not involve the conscious part of the brain. They protect the body from harm — for example, pulling your hand away from a hot object. The nerve pathway for a reflex is called a reflex arc:

Receptor → sensory neurone → relay neurone (in spinal cord) → motor neurone → effector

Key Fact

Reflex arcs bypass the brain, making responses faster. The pathway is: receptor → sensory neurone → relay neurone (spinal cord) → motor neurone → effector. This protects the body from danger.

Required Practical 7 involves investigating the effect of a factor on human reaction time. A common method is the ruler drop test: one person holds a ruler vertically, the other person catches it when released. The distance the ruler falls is related to reaction time — a shorter distance means a faster reaction. Variables such as caffeine, practice, or distraction can be investigated as independent variables.

The brain is the main coordination centre. It receives impulses from receptors and sends impulses to effectors. Different regions of the brain have different functions: the cerebral cortex (consciousness, thought, memory), the cerebellum (balance and coordination) and the medulla (unconscious activities like breathing and heart rate).
lessons.exam_tip_html: When describing a reflex arc, always list the components in order and include the type of neurone at each stage. A common mistake is forgetting the relay neurone or putting the brain instead of the spinal cord. Also remember: reflexes are involuntary — they bypass the conscious brain for speed.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Homeostasis maintains stable internal conditions using receptors, coordination centres and effectors, often via negative feedback.
  • The nervous system pathway: stimulus → receptor → sensory neurone → relay neurone → motor neurone → effector → response.
  • Reflex arcs are rapid, involuntary responses that bypass the brain (through the spinal cord) to protect the body.

lessons.title: The Endocrine System and Blood Glucose Control
lessons.description: How hormones coordinate body functions, and how the pancreas controls blood glucose levels.
lessons.content_html:
The Endocrine System

The endocrine system is made up of glands that produce hormones. Hormones are chemical messengers secreted directly into the blood and carried to target organs where they produce an effect. Compared to the nervous system, hormonal responses are slower but longer-lasting and act on a wider area.

The pituitary gland in the brain is called the “master gland” because it produces hormones that act on other glands, stimulating them to release their own hormones. Key endocrine glands include:

  • Pituitary gland (brain) — produces growth hormone, FSH, LH, ADH, TSH.
  • Thyroid gland (neck) — produces thyroxine, which regulates metabolic rate.
  • Pancreas — produces insulin and glucagon to control blood glucose.
  • Adrenal glands (above kidneys) — produce adrenaline for the “fight or flight” response.
  • Ovaries — produce oestrogen and progesterone.
  • Testes — produce testosterone.
Key Fact

The pituitary gland is the “master gland” — it produces hormones that control other glands. Hormones travel in the blood to target organs and produce slower but longer-lasting responses than nerves.

Blood Glucose Control

Blood glucose concentration is monitored and controlled by the pancreas. When blood glucose rises (e.g. after eating), the pancreas releases insulin. Insulin causes glucose to move from the blood into cells, and stimulates the liver to convert glucose into glycogen for storage. This lowers blood glucose back to normal.

When blood glucose falls too low (e.g. during exercise or between meals), the pancreas releases glucagon. Glucagon causes the liver to convert glycogen back into glucose, which is released into the blood. This raises blood glucose back to normal. This is a classic example of negative feedback.

Key Fact

Insulin lowers blood glucose (glucose → glycogen in liver). Glucagon raises blood glucose (glycogen → glucose from liver). Both are produced by the pancreas in a negative feedback loop.

Type 1 diabetes is a condition where the pancreas produces little or no insulin. It is usually diagnosed in childhood, is not linked to lifestyle, and is treated with insulin injections. The patient must also monitor their diet and blood glucose levels.

Type 2 diabetes is where the body’s cells no longer respond to insulin properly (insulin resistance). It is linked to obesity and lifestyle factors. It is treated with a carbohydrate-controlled diet, increased exercise and sometimes medication. Type 2 diabetes is becoming more common worldwide due to rising obesity levels.

The nervous system transmits electrical impulses along neurones for fast, short-lived, localised responses. The endocrine system uses hormones carried in the blood for slower, longer-lasting, widespread responses. Both systems work together to coordinate body functions — for example, the hypothalamus in the brain links the two systems.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When explaining blood glucose control, always include the hormone, the gland that produces it, and the specific effect on the liver. A common mistake is confusing insulin and glucagon — remember: insulin = glucose goes in to cells (blood glucose decreases).
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The endocrine system uses hormones (chemical messengers) in the blood; the pituitary gland is the “master gland”.
  • Insulin (high glucose → glycogen) and glucagon (low glucose → glucose) control blood glucose via negative feedback.
  • Type 1 diabetes: no insulin produced (treat with injections). Type 2: insulin resistance (treat with diet/exercise).

lessons.title: Hormones in Reproduction and Contraception
lessons.description: The menstrual cycle hormones, hormonal and non-hormonal contraception, and fertility treatments.
lessons.content_html:
Hormones and the Menstrual Cycle

The menstrual cycle is a roughly 28-day cycle controlled by four key hormones that interact through feedback mechanisms:

  • FSH (follicle-stimulating hormone) — released by the pituitary gland. It causes an egg to mature in a follicle in the ovary and stimulates the ovaries to produce oestrogen.
  • Oestrogen — produced by the ovaries. It causes the uterus lining to thicken and build up with blood vessels. At high levels, it stimulates LH release and inhibits FSH.
  • LH (luteinising hormone) — released by the pituitary gland. A surge of LH triggers ovulation around day 14.
  • Progesterone — produced by the empty follicle after ovulation. It maintains the uterus lining. If no fertilisation occurs, progesterone levels drop, the lining breaks down, and menstruation begins.
Key Fact

The menstrual cycle: FSH (matures egg + stimulates oestrogen) → Oestrogen (thickens lining + triggers LH surge) → LH (triggers ovulation on day 14) → Progesterone (maintains lining). All four hormones interact via feedback.

Contraception

Contraception can be hormonal or non-hormonal:

Oral contraceptive pill — contains hormones (oestrogen and/or progesterone) that inhibit FSH production, preventing egg maturation and ovulation. The combined pill uses both hormones; the progesterone-only pill has fewer side effects.

Contraceptive injection, implant or skin patch — release progesterone slowly over weeks or months, providing long-term contraception without daily action.

Intrauterine device (IUD) — a device inserted into the uterus. Hormonal IUDs release progesterone; copper IUDs are non-hormonal and prevent implantation.

Barrier methods — condoms (male and female) and diaphragms physically prevent sperm from reaching the egg. Condoms also protect against sexually transmitted infections (STIs).

Spermicidal agents — chemicals that kill or disable sperm, often used with barrier methods.

Surgical methods — sterilisation (cutting or tying the fallopian tubes or vas deferens) is permanent and very effective.

Abstinence or natural family planning — avoiding intercourse during the fertile window. Less reliable than other methods.

Key Fact

Hormonal contraceptives work by inhibiting FSH (preventing egg maturation) and/or preventing ovulation. Only barrier methods (condoms) protect against both pregnancy and STIs.

Fertility Treatments

Some couples have difficulty conceiving. Fertility treatments include:

  • FSH and LH injections — given to women who do not produce enough FSH naturally, stimulating egg maturation and ovulation.
  • IVF (in vitro fertilisation) — the mother is given FSH and LH to stimulate multiple eggs, which are collected and fertilised with sperm outside the body. One or two embryos are then transferred to the uterus.

IVF raises ethical issues: it is emotionally and physically demanding, expensive, has a low success rate, and can result in multiple pregnancies. Unused embryos may be destroyed, which some people object to on moral or religious grounds.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When describing the menstrual cycle, always state which gland produces each hormone and its specific effect. A 6-mark question may ask you to explain the role of hormones in the cycle — structure your answer chronologically (FSH first, then oestrogen, LH, progesterone) and mention feedback interactions.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Four hormones control the menstrual cycle: FSH (egg maturation), oestrogen (lining thickens, triggers LH), LH (ovulation), progesterone (maintains lining).
  • Hormonal contraceptives inhibit FSH/prevent ovulation; barrier methods (condoms) also protect against STIs.
  • IVF involves hormonal stimulation, egg collection, laboratory fertilisation and embryo transfer.

lessons.title: Reproduction, Meiosis and DNA
lessons.description: Sexual and asexual reproduction, how meiosis produces gametes, and the structure of DNA.
lessons.content_html:
Sexual and Asexual Reproduction

There are two types of reproduction. Sexual reproduction involves the fusion (joining) of male and female gametes (sperm and egg). The offspring are genetically different from each other and from both parents, because they receive a random mix of genetic material. This genetic variation is important for natural selection.

Asexual reproduction involves only one parent and no fusion of gametes. The offspring are genetically identical to the parent — they are clones. Asexual reproduction occurs through mitosis. Many plants and some animals (e.g. bacteria, starfish) can reproduce asexually.

Key Fact

Sexual reproduction: two parents, gametes fuse, offspring are genetically varied. Asexual reproduction: one parent, mitosis only, offspring are clones. Variation in sexual reproduction is important for natural selection and survival.

Meiosis

Meiosis is the type of cell division that produces gametes (sex cells). It takes place in the reproductive organs (ovaries and testes). Before meiosis, the DNA replicates. The cell then divides twice, producing four genetically different haploid cells, each with half the chromosome number (23 in humans).

When two gametes fuse at fertilisation, the full chromosome number is restored (46 in humans). The resulting cell is called a zygote, which then divides by mitosis to form an embryo.

Mitosis: one division, produces 2 identical diploid cells, used for growth and repair. Meiosis: two divisions, produces 4 different haploid cells (gametes), used for sexual reproduction. Both start with DNA replication, but meiosis shuffles genetic material, creating variation.

DNA Structure

DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) is a polymer made up of two strands twisted into a double helix. DNA is found in the nucleus of cells, arranged into structures called chromosomes. Humans have 23 pairs of chromosomes (46 total).

A gene is a short section of DNA on a chromosome. Each gene codes for a particular sequence of amino acids, which are assembled into a specific protein. The entire set of genetic material in an organism is called its genome.

Key Fact

DNA is a double helix found in chromosomes in the nucleus. A gene is a section of DNA that codes for a protein. Humans have 23 pairs of chromosomes. The Human Genome Project mapped all human DNA.

The Human Genome Project was an international effort to map every gene in the human genome. Understanding the genome helps scientists identify genes linked to specific diseases, develop personalised medicines, and trace human migration patterns and evolutionary relationships.
lessons.exam_tip_html: A common exam error is confusing mitosis and meiosis. Remember: mitosis = identical cells (2 diploid), meiosis = gametes (4 haploid, genetically different). Always state the number of divisions and the number/type of cells produced.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Sexual reproduction produces genetically varied offspring via gamete fusion; asexual reproduction produces clones via mitosis.
  • Meiosis: two divisions, four genetically different haploid cells. Mitosis: one division, two identical diploid cells.
  • DNA is a double helix in chromosomes; genes are sections of DNA that code for proteins.

practice_questions.text: Compare sexual and asexual reproduction, and discuss why organisms that reproduce sexually may have an advantage in changing environments.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (5-6): Detailed comparison with evolutionary reasoning.
Sexual reproduction involves two parents and fusion of gametes; asexual involves one parent and no gametes (1). Sexual reproduction produces genetically varied offspring; asexual produces clones (1). In a changing environment, some offspring from sexual reproduction may have characteristics better suited to the new conditions (1). This variation means some are more likely to survive and reproduce (natural selection) (1). In asexual reproduction, all offspring are identical, so if the environment changes unfavourably, all may be affected (1). However, asexual reproduction is faster and only needs one parent, which is advantageous in stable environments (1).

lessons.title: Genetic Inheritance and Inherited Disorders
lessons.description: Dominant and recessive alleles, Punnett squares, and inherited conditions like cystic fibrosis.
lessons.content_html:
Alleles and Inheritance

Most characteristics are controlled by several genes working together (polygenic). Some characteristics are controlled by a single gene with two forms called alleles. You inherit one allele from each parent, giving you two alleles for each gene.

If the two alleles are the same, the individual is homozygous for that gene. If they are different, the individual is heterozygous. A dominant allele is always expressed when present (shown by a capital letter, e.g. B). A recessive allele is only expressed when two copies are present (bb).

Key Fact

Genotype = the combination of alleles (e.g. Bb). Phenotype = the physical characteristic expressed (e.g. brown eyes). Dominant alleles only need one copy to be expressed; recessive alleles need two copies (homozygous recessive).

Punnett Squares and Genetic Diagrams

A Punnett square is used to show the possible combinations of alleles in offspring. For example, if both parents are heterozygous (Bb):

The offspring ratios would be: \(\frac{1}{4}\) BB, \(\frac{2}{4}\) Bb, \(\frac{1}{4}\) bb. This gives a 3:1 phenotype ratio (3 dominant : 1 recessive).

A couple are both carriers of cystic fibrosis (genotype Ff). What is the probability of their child having cystic fibrosis?

Parent genotypes: Ff × Ff. The Punnett square gives: FF, Ff, Ff, ff. Only ff has cystic fibrosis. So the probability is \(\frac{1}{4}\) or 25%. Note: each child has the same probability, regardless of previous children.

Inherited Disorders

Some disorders are caused by faulty alleles inherited from parents:

Cystic fibrosis is a disorder of cell membranes caused by a recessive allele (f). A person must inherit two copies (ff) to be affected. A carrier (Ff) has one copy but does not show symptoms. It causes thick, sticky mucus to build up in the lungs and digestive system.

Polydactyly is caused by a dominant allele. It causes extra fingers or toes. Only one copy of the dominant allele is needed to have the condition (Dd or DD).

Key Fact

Cystic fibrosis = recessive disorder (need ff to be affected; Ff = carrier). Polydactyly = dominant disorder (need only one D allele). Use Punnett squares to predict offspring ratios.

During IVF, embryos can be screened for genetic disorders before being implanted. This allows parents to select embryos that do not carry the faulty allele. However, embryo screening is controversial — some people argue it prevents suffering, while others believe it is unethical to select embryos or that it could lead to “designer babies.”

Sex Determination

In humans, sex is determined by the 23rd pair of chromosomes: XX = female, XY = male. A Punnett square shows there is a 50% chance of each sex. The Y chromosome carries the SRY gene, which triggers male development.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Always show your Punnett square working clearly in the exam — even if the question doesn’t explicitly ask for one. Label parent genotypes, gametes, and offspring ratios. Remember to express probabilities as fractions, percentages or ratios. A common mistake is saying “there is a 1 in 4 chance, so 1 out of 4 children will be affected” — each child independently has the same probability.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Alleles are different versions of a gene; dominant alleles are always expressed, recessive only when homozygous (bb).
  • Punnett squares predict offspring genotype and phenotype ratios (e.g. 3:1 from two heterozygous parents).
  • Cystic fibrosis is recessive (ff); polydactyly is dominant (Dd or DD). Sex is determined by XX (female) or XY (male).

lessons.title: Variation, Evolution and Natural Selection
lessons.description: The causes of variation, Darwin’s theory of natural selection, and evidence for evolution.
lessons.content_html:
Variation

Variation is the differences between individuals of the same species. It can be caused by:

  • Genetic variation — differences in DNA inherited from parents. Caused by sexual reproduction (meiosis shuffles genes) and mutations (random changes in DNA).
  • Environmental variation — differences caused by the conditions an organism lives in, e.g. diet, climate, lifestyle.
  • Combination — most characteristics (e.g. height, weight) are influenced by both genes and environment.
Key Fact

Variation is caused by genetics (inherited from parents), the environment (conditions), or both. Mutations are random changes in DNA that can introduce new alleles. Most mutations have no effect on the phenotype.

Evolution by Natural Selection

Evolution is the gradual change in inherited characteristics of a population over many generations. Charles Darwin proposed the theory of natural selection to explain how evolution occurs:

  1. Within a population, there is variation in characteristics due to genetic differences.
  2. Individuals with characteristics better suited to the environment are more likely to survive and reproduce (survival of the fittest).
  3. These individuals pass on the advantageous alleles to their offspring.
  4. Over many generations, the proportion of individuals with the advantageous characteristic increases.

Evidence for evolution comes from: fossils (show how organisms have changed over time), antibiotic-resistant bacteria (observed natural selection in action), and comparative anatomy (similar bone structures in different species suggest common ancestors). The fossil record is incomplete because not all organisms fossilise, and many fossils are destroyed by geological processes.

Key Fact

Natural selection: variation → survival of the fittest → advantageous alleles passed on → frequency increases over generations. Evidence includes fossils, resistant bacteria and comparative anatomy.

Selective Breeding and Extinction

Selective breeding (artificial selection) is when humans choose organisms with desirable traits to breed together. Examples include breeding cows for higher milk yield, dogs for specific characteristics, and crops for disease resistance. A disadvantage is that it reduces genetic variation within the population, making it more vulnerable to disease.

Extinction occurs when a species dies out completely. Causes include: new predators or diseases, environmental changes, loss of habitat, competition, and catastrophic events. Carl Linnaeus developed the classification system that organises living things into groups based on shared characteristics: kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When explaining natural selection, always follow the four-step process: variation → competition → survival of the fittest → reproduction and passing on alleles. Use a specific example if possible (e.g. antibiotic resistance in bacteria or peppered moths). Don’t say organisms “choose” to evolve — evolution is not a conscious process.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Variation is caused by genetics, environment, or both; mutations introduce new alleles.
  • Natural selection: variation → survival of the fittest → advantageous alleles passed to offspring → population changes over generations.
  • Selective breeding chooses desirable traits but reduces genetic variation; extinction occurs when a species cannot adapt.

lessons.title: Genetic Engineering and Ecology
lessons.description: Covers genetic engineering (4.6.4), benefits and risks of genetic engineering, ecosystems and com...
lessons.content_html:
Genetic Engineering

Genetic engineering is a process where scientists modify the genetic material of an organism. A gene that codes for a useful characteristic is “cut” from one organism’s DNA and inserted into another organism’s genome. The organism that receives the new gene is called a genetically modified organism (GMO).

Key Fact

In genetic engineering, enzymes are used to isolate the required gene. This gene is then inserted into a vector (such as a bacterial plasmid or virus) which carries it into the cells of the target organism. The organism’s cells then produce the desired protein.

The process of genetic engineering follows a clear sequence of steps. First, the gene that produces the desired characteristic is identified and isolated using restriction enzymes, which cut DNA at specific recognition sequences. The gene is then inserted into a vector — typically a small ring of bacterial DNA called a plasmid. The vector carries the gene into the host organism’s cells, where it is incorporated into the DNA and expressed to produce the desired protein.

One of the most important applications is the production of human insulin by genetically modified bacteria. The human insulin gene is inserted into bacterial plasmids, and the bacteria then produce insulin in large quantities. This replaced the older method of extracting insulin from pig or cow pancreases, which sometimes caused allergic reactions in patients.

GM crops have been engineered to be resistant to insect attack or to produce higher yields. For example, Bt corn contains a gene from a soil bacterium that produces a natural insecticide, reducing the need for chemical pesticides. Golden rice has been modified to produce beta-carotene (a source of vitamin A) to help combat vitamin A deficiency in developing countries.

Benefits and Risks of Genetic Engineering

Genetic engineering has significant potential benefits. In agriculture, GM crops can increase food production by improving resistance to pests, disease and herbicides. This can help feed a growing world population. In medicine, genetic engineering allows large-scale production of useful proteins such as insulin and growth hormone.

However, there are concerns. Some people worry that GM crops could have unknown effects on human health if consumed over long periods. There are also ecological concerns — genes from GM plants could spread to wild populations through cross-pollination, potentially creating “superweeds” that are resistant to herbicides. Ethical concerns exist about whether it is right to modify the genes of living organisms, particularly when it comes to genetic modification of animals or potential future modifications of human embryos.

Key Fact

You are expected to evaluate the benefits and risks of genetic engineering. Benefits include: disease-resistant crops, higher yields, medical protein production. Risks include: unknown long-term health effects, gene transfer to wild populations, and ethical concerns.

Ecosystems and Communities

An ecosystem is the interaction of a community of living organisms (biotic) with the non-living (abiotic) parts of their environment. Ecosystems can range in size from a small pond to an entire ocean. Within an ecosystem, organisms are organised into levels.

A community is all the populations of different species living and interacting together in an area. A population is all the organisms of one species in a given area. A habitat is the place where an organism lives. Each species has its own role within the community, known as its niche.

Abiotic factors are non-living conditions that influence where organisms can live. These include light intensity, temperature, moisture level, soil pH and mineral content, wind speed and direction, and carbon dioxide levels (for plants) or oxygen levels (for aquatic organisms).

Biotic factors are living factors that affect organisms in an ecosystem. These include availability of food, the introduction of new predators or competitors, and the arrival of new pathogens (disease-causing organisms). Changes in any biotic or abiotic factor can affect the distribution and population size of species in a community.

Competition and Interdependence

Organisms within a community compete for resources. Animals compete for food, territory, mates and water. Plants compete for light, water, space and mineral ions from the soil. If two species are competing for the same niche, one will usually out-compete the other. Within a community, species depend on each other for food, shelter, seed dispersal and pollination — this is called interdependence. If one species is removed, the whole community can be affected.

A stable community is one where all the species and environmental factors are in balance so that population sizes remain roughly the same. Examples include tropical rainforests and ancient oak woodlands. In these ecosystems, the populations of predators and prey, producers and consumers are balanced over time.

Feeding Relationships and Trophic Levels

Trophic levels describe the position of an organism in a food chain. Producers (usually green plants or algae) are at trophic level 1 — they photosynthesise to make their own food. Primary consumers (herbivores) eat the producers and are at trophic level 2. Secondary consumers (carnivores) eat the primary consumers and are at trophic level 3. Tertiary consumers are at trophic level 4.

Key Fact

Producers are the starting point of all food chains because they transfer energy from the Sun into biomass through photosynthesis. All consumers depend — directly or indirectly — on producers for their energy.

Predators kill and eat other animals (their prey). In a stable community, the populations of predators and prey rise and fall in cycles. When the prey population increases, more food is available for predators, so the predator population also increases. This then causes the prey population to fall (more are eaten), which in turn causes the predator population to decline. This repeating pattern is known as the predator-prey cycle.

Decomposers (mainly bacteria and fungi) break down dead plant and animal matter through the process of decay. This returns mineral ions and nutrients to the soil, where they can be taken up again by plants. Decomposition is faster in warm, moist, aerobic conditions. Decomposers are essential for nutrient cycling in ecosystems.

Energy is transferred along food chains, but not all energy passes from one trophic level to the next. At each level, energy is lost to the surroundings through life processes — organisms use energy for movement, keeping warm, and other metabolic reactions. Energy is also lost in waste products (faeces and urine) and through respiration. This is why food chains rarely have more than four or five trophic levels — there is not enough energy left to support organisms beyond that point.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When answering questions about genetic engineering and ecology, always reference specific examples and explain both benefits and potential risks or limitations.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Complete specification content needed for accurate lesson generation
  • Genetic engineering and ecology are interconnected topics in modern biology
  • Exam questions require specific examples and balanced evaluation

lessons.title: Ecosystems, Biodiversity and Human Impact
lessons.description: Food chains, nutrient cycling, biodiversity, and how human activities affect ecosystems.
lessons.content_html:
Communities and Ecosystems

An ecosystem is the interaction of a community of living organisms (biotic factors) with the non-living (abiotic) parts of their environment. A community includes all the organisms of different species living together. A population is all the organisms of one species in a habitat.

Abiotic factors include light intensity, temperature, moisture, soil pH and mineral content, wind speed and direction, and availability of carbon dioxide and oxygen. Biotic factors include availability of food, new predators, new pathogens and competition between organisms.

Key Fact

Ecosystems consist of biotic (living) and abiotic (non-living) factors. In a stable community, the populations of all species are balanced. Changes to abiotic or biotic factors can destabilise a community.

Food Chains and Interdependence

Organisms in a community depend on each other for food, shelter and other resources. This is called interdependence. Food chains show the flow of energy from producers to consumers:

Producer → Primary consumer → Secondary consumer → Tertiary consumer

Producers (plants) convert light energy into chemical energy through photosynthesis. Consumers obtain energy by eating other organisms. If one species in a food chain is removed, it affects all the other organisms — this is called interdependence.

Carbon is recycled through ecosystems. Plants take in \(CO_2\) for photosynthesis and use it to make glucose. Animals eat plants and release \(CO_2\) through respiration. When organisms die, decomposers (bacteria and fungi) break down the dead material, releasing \(CO_2\) through respiration. Combustion of fossil fuels also releases \(CO_2\).

Biodiversity and Human Impact

Biodiversity is the variety of different species in an ecosystem. High biodiversity makes ecosystems more stable and resilient to change. However, human activities are rapidly reducing biodiversity worldwide.

Human activities that reduce biodiversity include:

  • Deforestation — clearing forests for agriculture and building destroys habitats.
  • Pollution — land, water and air pollution damage habitats and kill organisms.
  • Global warming — rising temperatures alter habitats and cause species migration or extinction.
  • Overexploitation — overfishing, hunting and intensive farming reduce populations.
Key Fact

Biodiversity is being reduced by deforestation, pollution, global warming and overexploitation. Conservation programmes, breeding programmes, seed banks and habitat restoration help maintain biodiversity.

Strategies to maintain biodiversity include: breeding programmes for endangered species, protection of rare habitats (e.g. national parks, SSSIs), reintroduction of hedgerows and field margins in agricultural areas, seed banks to preserve genetic diversity, and reducing deforestation and carbon emissions. Scientists also use techniques like quadrats and transects to sample and monitor biodiversity in ecosystems.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When explaining the impact of removing one species from a food chain, always trace the effect both up and down the chain. For example, if a primary consumer is removed, the producer population may increase (less grazing) while the secondary consumer population decreases (less food). Always link back to interdependence.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Ecosystems = biotic + abiotic factors; organisms are interdependent through food chains and nutrient cycling.
  • Carbon is recycled through photosynthesis, respiration, decomposition and combustion.
  • Human activities (deforestation, pollution, global warming) reduce biodiversity; conservation strategies help protect it.

practice_questions.text: Describe two abiotic factors that could affect a community.
practice_questions.marks: Temperature — affects the rate of enzyme-controlled reactions / growth (1). Light intensity — affects the rate of photosynthesis in producers (1). Accept: moisture, soil pH, wind, CO2.

practice_questions.text: Explain how carbon is recycled in an ecosystem.
practice_questions.marks: Plants absorb CO2 from the atmosphere during photosynthesis to produce glucose (1). Animals eat plants and release CO2 through respiration (1). When organisms die, decomposers break down the remains and release CO2 through respiration (1). Accept: combustion of fossil fuels releases CO2.

practice_questions.text: Explain why high biodiversity is important for the stability of an ecosystem.
practice_questions.marks: High biodiversity means there are many different species (1). If one species is lost, other species can fulfil a similar role in the food chain (1). This means the food web is less likely to collapse (1). The ecosystem is more resilient to changes in environmental conditions (1).

practice_questions.text: Discuss the impact of deforestation on biodiversity and the carbon cycle.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (5-6): Detailed discussion linking both concepts.
Deforestation destroys habitats, reducing the number of species that can live there (1). Many organisms lose their food sources and shelter, leading to population decline or extinction (1). This reduces biodiversity (1). Trees absorb CO2 during photosynthesis; removing trees means less CO2 is absorbed from the atmosphere (1). Burning or decomposing trees releases stored carbon as CO2 (1). This contributes to increased atmospheric CO2 and enhanced global warming (1).

practice_questions.text: Describe one method scientists use to estimate population size in a habitat.
practice_questions.marks: Scientists use quadrats placed randomly in the habitat (1). They count the organisms in each quadrat and use the data to estimate total population across the whole area (1). Accept: transects, capture-recapture.

glossary_terms.definition: A community of living organisms interacting with the non-living parts of their environment.
All the populations of different species living and interacting together in a habitat.
All the organisms of one species living in a habitat at a particular time.
Non-living factors that affect a community, such as light, temperature, moisture and soil pH.
Living factors that affect a community, such as food availability, predators and competition.
The reliance of organisms on each other for survival.
Organisms that make their own food using photosynthesis.
Organisms that eat other organisms for energy.
Microorganisms that break down dead organic matter.
The variety of different species of organisms on Earth or within an ecosystem.
